subject: Chemistry
title: Gallium: The First Predicted Element
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Gallium: The First Predicted Element.

hook.text: In 1875, a French chemist found a new element in zinc ore. It matched what Mendeleev had predicted six years earlier.

buildup.text: Paul Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered gallium. He measured its density at 4.7 g/cm³.

discovery.text: Mendeleev had predicted a density of 5.9. He told Lecoq to measure again—and Lecoq found Mendeleev was right.

twist.text: Lecoq named it gallium after Gallia, Latin for France. Some suspect he also hid a pun on his own name.

climax.text: Gallium melts at 29.7°C—it liquefies in your hand. It's now used in semiconductors and LEDs.

punchline.text: Predicted before it was found. Gallium proved the table right.

quiz.question: What was remarkable about the discovery of gallium?
options: Mendeleev had predicted its properties before it was found
It was the first element discovered in France
It was found inside a meteorite

details.summary: French chemist Paul Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered gallium in 1875 using spectroscopy, confirming Mendeleev's eka-aluminum prediction from 1871..
details.whyItMatters: Gallium's discovery converted skeptics and established the periodic table's predictive power as scientific fact. Today gallium is essential in semiconductor chips, LEDs, and solar cells.
takeaways: Gallium was discovered through its unique spectral lines in zinc ore samples
Its properties matched Mendeleev's eka-aluminum predictions almost exactly
Gallium melts at just 29.8 degrees Celsius, below human body temperature

faq.question: How did Mendeleev correct the discoverer of gallium?
faq.answer: When de Boisbaudran first reported gallium's density as 4.7, Mendeleev wrote to him insisting it should be closer to 5.9 based on his prediction. De Boisbaudran re-measured with a purer sample and found 5.91, almost exactly matching Mendeleev's prediction. The predictor corrected the discoverer.

faq.question: Why is gallium used in modern technology despite being relatively obscure?
faq.answer: Gallium arsenide and gallium nitride are superior semiconductors for specific applications including high-frequency electronics, LEDs, laser diodes, and solar cells..
